verdicts.note: Attacked on two grounds. (1) The tax has never been collected (first payments 2029), so YES prevents a tax rather than cutting one; but the rubric's pole A is explicitly 'oppose new taxes (income, wealth...)' and pole B names the 'millionaires tax', so a vote on whether this tax takes effect is squarely on the axis. (2) Strength: the dossier shows the largest revenue effect of any measure ($11.4 billion over SFY 2027-2031 per OFM) plus a standing statutory ban on any state or local income tax; -2 holds. Citations S1, S3, S5, S8 each support the basis.

Closest call. Direction: pole A is 'skepticism of state mandates', pole B 'state mandates'; a state statute that removes a tax option from every county, city and local jurisdiction (S5 sec. 4(3)) is a state rule over local discretion, so +1 is the right sign even though the yes campaign frames the measure as 'restores your right to decide' (S4) -- that is about voters versus the Legislature, not about which level of government decides. Strongest counterargument: a NO vote does not give local governments the option either, because RCW 1.90.100(1) (I-2111) already bars local income taxes and ESSB 6346 exempted only the state tax (S9, S7); the practical difference for localities is the initiative's broader 'income' definition, 'measured by' clause and liberal-construction rule (S5). That supports keeping strength 1 rather than 2, not dropping the mapping, because the measure's own text and ballot subject ('state and local taxes', S1) put the local ban on the ballot. Director may prefer to drop it if a near-zero practical change should carry no lean.

Attacked as double counting the taxes mapping, since the measure contains no audit, performance or spending rule and its spending effect runs entirely through revenue. Upheld at 1 because the dossier carries separate spending evidence: the yes statement's central case is accountability for past spending (dedicated-fund transfers, unkept capital-gains commitments, 'demonstrate they can keep the commitments', S4), and the no case and OFM/legislative intent tie the revenue to program expansions (free school meals, child care, WFTC expansion; S3, S8). This mirrors the primary's practice of mapping spending +1 for levies that fund program expansion. Strength 2 would overstate it.

Checked against the dossier: what_it_does matches the repeal and the sec. 4 prohibition (S5) and correctly says the sales/B&O/WFTC changes are not repealed (S2, S5); cost_line figures ($11.4 billion SFY 2027-2031, $377 million fair start for kids, about $150 million agency savings, no local revenue effect) match OFM (S3). pro_summary and con_summary name the pamphlet signatories as printed (S4) and attribute every claim. The con_summary deliberately omits the statement's '$13 billion over four years' and '460,000 families' figures, which conflict with OFM's $11.4 billion estimate and the Attorney General's statement that the accompanying credits and exemptions remain (S2, S3); the dossier records both claims with that context. Neither summary assigns the pamphlet authors to a PDC committee, which the sources do not establish.

Attacked on direction, strength and the basis wording. Direction: the measure restores records copies within 10 business days covering all student-specific files, including health and mental health counseling records, brings back three prior-notice medical rights, widens opt-outs to any survey, assignment or activity on the listed topics, and removes the policies-and-procedures qualifier on materials access (S5, S2, S6). That is pole A. The 2025 text kept FERPA timing, chapter 70.02 RCW health confidentiality and opt-outs limited to the federal PPRA scope (S7, S6), which is pole B. Evidence the other way: Gov. Ferguson and the no statement say it removes parents' rights (S17, S4), and the crime-notice trigger changes from 'upon receipt of a report' to when a criminal action 'is deemed to have been committed' (S9, S5). The rights it drops (bullying complaints, enrollment, language access, special education) are not notification, records or opt-out rights, and the AG says the 2025 list restated rights found elsewhere in law (S2). These points do not move the measure's center of gravity, so -2 holds. The basis originally said 'every change' on notice moves toward pole A, which overstated given the crime-notice trigger; it now says 'nearly every change' and names the exception. All four citations exist in the dossier frontmatter and support the basis.

Three fixes, applied to scoring/measures.json in the same commit. (1) what_it_does listed special education among 'entries added in 2025', but the OPR list of 2025 additions (S6) does not include it, and it omitted that the nondiscrimination entry is replaced by an assurance against discrimination based on the family's religious beliefs (S5 sec. 1(3)(i), S2); now 'entries in the 2025 version' with the replacement stated. (2) 'instead of 45' now reads 'instead of up to 45 days' (S2, S6). (3) pro_summary called three signers 'parent advocates'; only Alesha Perkins signs as a parent and education advocate, Amy Sousa as a women's rights advocate and Jess Grant as a member of Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender (S4); now named that way. Checked and supported: cost_line matches OFM (S3); con_summary signers match S4 and its claims are attributed paraphrases; 'weaken immediate notice' is milder than the statement's 'ending ... requirement' but attributed and consistent with the dossier's context note (S7 sec. 601); the pro_summary's gender-identity claim is attributed to the statement.

Attacked on direction, strength and applicability. The rubric's social pole A names 'Sex-based eligibility for girls' and women's sports' and pole B names 'Trans participation in sports by gender identity'. The measure writes the first into statute (S1, S5), and the AG says it 'would generally prevent transgender girls from participating on girls' sports teams' (S2). It replaces WIAA Rule 18.16.0, a gender-identity participation rule (S7). It has no other subject, so -2 is not overstated. No dossier evidence points the other way: the opposition's privacy and exam arguments describe how the measure works, not a different direction on the axis. Citations S1, S5, S2 and S7 exist and support the basis.

Three fixes plus one precision edit, applied to scoring/measures.json in the same commit. (1) pro_summary called signers 'parent advocates'; only Alesha Perkins is a parent and education advocate and Jess Grant signs as a member of Democrats for an Informed Approach to Gender (S4); now named that way. (2) pro_summary said the measure 'protects fairness and opportunities'; the statement says 'protect fairness in girls' sports' and 'affirm the hard-fought rights established through Title IX' (S4); now 'fairness in girls' sports and the rights established by Title IX'. (3) cost_line said districts 'would have' costs; OFM says districts 'may also incur costs' (S3); now 'may incur'. (4) what_it_does now quotes 'normal endogenously produced testosterone levels' (S5) instead of 'natural testosterone levels'. Checked and supported: the $21,000 OSPI figure and no revenue effect (S3); coverage of public K-12 schools and WIAA private schools (S2); verification for every student entering a female-only competition (S5, S2); replacement of WIAA Rule 18.16.0 (S7, S8). con_summary signers match S4 and its claims are attributed paraphrases.

review_notes: Fresh read of the dossier and rubric. Applicable measure axes are taxes, spending, local-control, social and parental-rights; the dossier holds no evidence on social or parental-rights (the Planned Parenthood Advocates signer on the con statement is a signatory, not policy content), so no missing mappings are proposed. Factual points re-checked while reviewing: the $1 million standard deduction is per individual, shared by spouses or registered domestic partners (ESSB 6346 sec. 314), which the dossier states precisely; OFM's prose $279,000 vs table $271,000 DSHS discrepancy is recorded, not resolved. IL26-001 and IL26-638 (independent pass, 2026-10-08): four candidate missing mappings were considered and none is proposed. social for IL26-001: section 1 strikes the 2025 list entry that names gender identity and substitutes a religious-belief assurance (S5, S2), but the prohibition stays in RCW 28A.642.010, which the measure does not amend (S7); the gender-identity disclosure dispute is in the campaign arguments only (S4), so at most a low-confidence inference. local-control for IL26-638: the opposition says decisions are taken from schools and athletic associations (S15), but the WIAA says state law already bars a sex-based rule and OSPI has steered districts to gender-identity participation since 2012 (S8, S6); the measure swaps one statewide standard for another, with no clear direction. local-control for IL26-001 rests only on the removed 'policies and procedures' qualifier on materials access (S6, S2), too narrow and partly double counting parental-rights. parental-rights for IL26-638: no notice, records or opt-out content (S5). spending: no basis for either (OFM: no state fiscal impact for IL26-001, one-time $21,000 for IL26-638, S3).
